old_exact_step: 1.1 Fix a complementary region $R_0$. For any other region $R$, choose a path from an interior point of $R_0$ to an interior point of $R$, perturb it to avoid vertices and cross edges transversely, and color $R$ by the parity of the number of crossed edges. The parity is independent of the path: the symmetric difference of two paths is a finite closed edge-set modulo two. Every vertex of $P$ has even degree, so this edge-set decomposes into simple graph cycles: follow unused edges until returning to the start, split any repeated-vertex trail at that vertex, and repeat with the remaining edges. Each such cycle is a simple piecewise-smooth closed curve. Choose disjoint small disks about its vertices, away from the finitely many test-curve intersections, and round the cycle's corners inside those disks; this preserves the number of intersections with the test curve. By [F2], the rounded smooth Jordan curve separates $S^2$ into two sides. A closed test curve switches sides at every transverse intersection and returns to its starting side, so it crosses each rounded cycle evenly and hence crosses the original edge cycle evenly. Summing over the finite decomposition shows that it crosses the symmetric-difference edge-set evenly, proving path independence. [given, F1, F2, construct]
replacement_exact_step: 1.1 Fix a point $x_0$ in a complementary region $R_0$. First decompose the edges of $P$ into finitely many edge-disjoint simple cycles. In a nonempty remaining even-degree graph, follow unused edges until a vertex first repeats; the segment between its two occurrences is a simple cycle, including a loop edge as a one-edge cycle. Removing that cycle subtracts two incident half-edges at each of its vertices and leaves every degree even. Repeat until no edge remains. This terminates because each removal deletes an edge; a vertex-free circle is already one cycle. Now choose two piecewise-smooth paths $\alpha,\beta$ from $x_0$ to the same point in a region $R$, avoiding the finitely many vertices and meeting open edges transversely in finitely many points. Their concatenation $\gamma=\alpha*\beta^{-1}$ is a closed test path; it need not be embedded or be an edge-path of $P$. Its intersections are counted with traversal multiplicity, so $I(\gamma,P)=I(\alpha,P)+I(\beta,P)$ modulo two. For each simple graph cycle, choose small vertex disks disjoint from the compact image of $\gamma$ and round that cycle inside them. The rounded cycle remains embedded and has exactly the same test-path intersections as its original edges. By [F2] it separates $S^2$ into two sides. Each transverse encounter switches the side occupied by $\gamma$, and a complete traversal returns to its initial side, even when the test path self-intersects or retraces an arc. Thus $\gamma$ meets each rounded cycle evenly. The graph cycles partition all open edges and $\gamma$ misses their vertices, so summing their intersection counts proves $I(\gamma,P)=0$ modulo two. Therefore $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have the same crossing parity. Coloring $R$ by this parity gives a well-defined function, independent also of the chosen endpoint inside $R$, since two such endpoints are joined within $R$ without crossing $P$. All decompositions, rounding choices and perturbations are finite; no choice axiom is used. [given, F1, F2, construct]
